articles.title: Google Maps starts showing live fuel prices across UK, to be powered by UK government's Fuel Finder scheme
articles.summary: Drivers across United Kingdom (UK) can now check real-time gas station prices on Google Maps.
articles.body: Drivers across United Kingdom (UK) can now check real-time gas station prices on Google Maps. This comes after the UK government announced partnership with search giant Google. AS per the release, drivers are set to save at the pump as near real-time petrol and diesel prices now appear on Google Maps. To checking local fuel prices, users need to open Google Maps and search for a forecourt nearby, with near real time prices for petrol and diesel displayed on the app.As per the official release, this marks the latest step in the government’s work to tackle the affordability crisis, after the VAT cut to electricity bills and a £2 cap on bus fares, giving families some breathing space with the cost of living.Minister for Energy Consumers Polly Billington said, "Tackling the affordability crisis is our first responsibility and for so many families and businesses, petrol and diesel are essential goods, not luxuries. Accessing the cheapest fuel should be simple, which is why it is a gamechanger for near real-time fuel prices to be shown on Google Maps for the first time in the UK, helping drivers to find the best deal and save money at the pump."Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey, said, "Getting the best price at the pump is now easier. This doesn’t fix everything; bills have gone up because of events in the Middle East. But we’re not powerless. And small changes like this, cutting tax on electricity bills and capping bus fares at £2 all help give families a bit of breathing space."What is UK government's Fuel Finder schemeUK Government claims that Fuel Finder scheme was created to help drivers get more competitive fuel prices following a recommendation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA). It added that an overwhelming majority of petrol stations are inputting data to Fuel Finder promptly, with around 99% of all fuel sold on UK roads now reflected.Since February, it has been compulsory for petrol stations across the UK to report the price of their fuel within 30 minutes of it changing or risk a fine – and the CMA can take action where there is evidence that petrol stations are not complying with the law.The data is already used by thousands of drivers across apps such as Waze, Petrol Prices, the AA, Confused.com and RAC Fuel Watch, and its integration with Google Maps will help millions more motorists find the best price at the pump.Sarah-Jayne Williams, Director of Global Product Partnerships for Geo at Google, said, "Navigating fuel rising costs shouldn’t add stress to everyday journeys. Integrating Fuel Finder data into Google Maps and Waze gives drivers visibility on nearby pump prices, helping drivers make intentional choices to help their budgets go further this winter."You use AI every day. articles.title: A Connecticut town paid $455,000 for a historic two-family home to create about 20 library parking spaces; a state preservation council has now voted to ask the attorney general to stop its demolition
articles.summary: A plan to demolish a historic house in Manchester, Connecticut, to make space for additional library parking has faced opposition from the state's
articles.body: A plan to demolish a historic house in Manchester, Connecticut, to make space for additional library parking has faced opposition from the state's Historic Preservation Council. The town purchased the two-family property for $455,000 in June 2026, intending to replace it with around 20 parking spaces. However, preservation officials have now voted to seek intervention from the state's attorney general to prevent the demolition, according to CT Insider.The property, located at 29-31 Eldridge Street, stands next to Manchester's new Main Street library. It is part of the Cheney Brothers Historic District, an area recognised as a National Historic Landmark in 1978. The house was originally built to accommodate workers employed at the Cheney Brothers silk mills.The town's decision to demolish the building drew objections from some residents and members of the local historical society. Their concerns ultimately led to a review by Connecticut's Historic Preservation Office.On Wednesday, the Historic Preservation Council unanimously voted to ask the attorney general to intervene under the Connecticut Environmental Protection Act. The law allows action against the 'unreasonable destruction' of protected resources. Although commonly used to protect natural resources, it can also be applied to historic buildings.House can be restoredDuring the council meeting, preservation advocates argued that the property should be repaired rather than demolished.According to Brad Schide, a member of Preservation Connecticut, restoring the house would be a more appropriate solution. “The structure should be rehabbed and maintained in its present configuration. That to us is the prudent and feasible alternative,” Schide said.Dave Goslin, a principal at Krosky Architects, also assessed the building. Goslin, whose firm handles preservation projects, rated its quality eight out of 10. He said the house had remained in relatively good condition considering its age, although renovations were necessary.“When it was built it was well built and it has held up pretty well over time. The conditions within the building are tired. It’s in need of renovations,” Goslin said.Goslin suggested that Manchester could sell the property to a developer interested in historic preservation. Such a buyer could restore the building and continue using it as a two-family residence.He also proposed another option that would allow the town to create some parking without removing the house. Under this plan, the garage would be demolished to make room for approximately 10 parking spaces. However, Goslin acknowledged that the arrangement would leave the property with a 'substandard' lot and effectively turn its backyard into a parking area.Why town wants to demolish?Manchester officials maintained that the house was in poor condition and that keeping it would create additional maintenance costs.Town Manager Steve Stephanou described the property as an eyesore and defended the proposed demolition. “We cannot afford to operate and maintain a structure that frankly has been blighted for some time,” Stephanou said.He added that the building had not been properly maintained over the years and that vehicles had previously been parked on its lawn.According to Stephanou, the new library already has 54 parking spaces included in its plans. The town expects parking demand to increase, and the additional 20 spaces could eventually be reserved for library employees. He also argued that removing the building would eliminate a blind spot at the rear of the parking lot.Concerns over historic districtPreservation advocates raised concerns beyond the future of this particular house. Schide warned that demolishing one historic property could encourage the removal of others in the neighbourhood.“We find it all the time. Buildings, as they are removed, it kind of encourages other removal. If there’s too much of that you lose everything," Schide said.He noted that Eldridge Street still retains much of its historic character and that preserving the house would help protect the wider district.Stephanou responded that Manchester had no intention of demolishing other historic buildings. He said the town would even sign an agreement preventing further removals.However, Andy Horowitz, a Historic Preservation Council member and the state historian, argued that the district's National Historic Landmark designation already provided a basis for protecting its buildings. “It’s hard to argue here unambiguously that it’s beyond repair,” Horowitz said. He maintained that the existing historic designation should be sufficient reason to oppose demolition.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: David Beckham’s UNICEF 7 Fund supported 406,400 children; its four-country projects reached their final year in 2024
articles.summary: When David Beckham launched 7: The David Beckham UNICEF Fund in February 2015, he set out to help protect vulnerable children and give them a better
articles.body: When David Beckham launched 7: The David Beckham UNICEF Fund in February 2015, he set out to help protect vulnerable children and give them a better chance of reaching their potential. The initiative went on to support work addressing violence, bullying, child marriage and barriers to education, particularly among girls. Its projects in Nepal, Indonesia, Uganda and El Salvador worked with schools, families, communities and governments to strengthen child protection and improve access to education. UNICEF UK’s 2024 annual report described that year as the final year for the fund’s then-current projects. The programme’s reported results offer a picture of what the initiative achieved, while also raising an important question: whether the systems and services strengthened through the projects can sustain those gains after the funded work ends.David Beckham’s 7 Fund for UNICEF: how the initiative developedUNICEF and Beckham announced the fund on 9 February 2015. It was designed to raise money and awareness for children facing violence, abuse, disease and barriers to education, with particular attention to those most at risk. The initiative was named after Beckham’s familiar shirt number and formed part of his commitment to use his public profile to support UNICEF’s work. UNICEF announced support for work in Nepal, Indonesia, Uganda and El Salvador in 2018, although its 2024 annual report describes the current four-country programme as having operated since 2019. El Salvador had also featured in the fund’s original 2015 launch. Beckham visited Indonesia in 2018 to meet children and learn about bullying and violence affecting their education.They addressed different problems according to local needs, from child marriage and school exclusion in Nepal to bullying in Indonesia and violence affecting children in Uganda and El Salvador. Rather than focusing only on immediate assistance, the programmes worked with schools, families and community organisations to strengthen protection systems and help children remain in or return to education. The distinction between the fund’s launch and its later projects matters when assessing its record. UNICEF UK’s 2024 annual report said the four-country projects had reached their final year and reported that the fund had supported 406,400 children. That milestone does not mean the wider fund or Beckham’s relationship with UNICEF ended in 2024. It means the specific programme described in those four countries had reached the end of its planned project period.Nepal and Uganda: supporting girls’ education and preventing violenceIn Nepal, the fund supported programmes in Madhesh Province, where child marriage and barriers to education can prevent girls from continuing their studies. According to UNICEF UK’s annual report, 21,723 girls who were out of school completed the Supporting Adolescent Girls’ Education programme. The nine-month initiative provided literacy and numeracy instruction to help participants enrol in formal schooling and continue their education. The report also said more than 50,000 children and adolescents received information and support relating to mental health and the harmful effects of child marriage. The fund also supported Rupantaran, a life skills programme intended to help adolescents build confidence and make informed decisions. One participant, Antima, was profiled by UNICEF as a girl from a large family who had left school because her family could not afford to keep her enrolled. She began selling snacks and now earns about NPR 700 a day, helping support her family and pay for her younger siblings’ education, according to the 7 Fund’s account. Her story illustrates the financial pressures that can contribute to school exclusion, although an individual account cannot establish how typical such outcomes are.The 7 Fund’s Uganda project page reports that more than 25,000 adolescents in Adjumani District participated in life skills sessions, although its headline gives a lower overall figure of more than 23,000 children reached through life skills programmes. More than 10,400 parents and caregivers received information about violence prevention and harmful practices that can affect school attendance and completion. The programme also supported teacher training and systems for tracking and reporting violence in schools. UNICEF has profiled young people who used life skills clubs as a route back into education and towards careers they hoped to pursue. Christine Manuela, for example, was reported to have begun nursing and midwifery training at Kuluva Hospital in Arua District after participating in a Girls Education Club supported by the fund.Indonesia and El Salvador: tackling bullying and creating safer spacesIn Indonesia, the fund supported efforts to address bullying and peer violence, which can make school an unsafe environment and disrupt children’s education. Beckham visited the country in March 2018, meeting children involved in anti-bullying initiatives. UNICEF reported that the programme encouraged students to speak up when they experienced or witnessed violence and to help create safer learning environments. The 7 Fund’s project account says more than 147,500 adolescents in Indonesia participated in polls about bullying and mental health. These consultations gave young people an opportunity to express their views on issues affecting them. The programme also sought to involve schools and local authorities in improving children’s safety. Such participation figures measure engagement with the initiative; they do not, by themselves, establish how much bullying declined or how many children stayed in school as a direct result.In El Salvador, the programme focused on child protection and safe places for children to learn, play and take part in community activities. It worked in municipalities including San Marcos and San Martín, supporting child protection services and efforts to make public spaces more suitable for children. The 7 Fund’s project page reports that more than 1,600 child protection workers and community leaders received training and that more than 28,500 children took part in sports and recreational activities in safer community spaces. UNICEF UK’s 2024 annual report gives a different figure for recreational activities, reporting more than 27,300 children, and says 41,351 children and adolescents benefited from the programme overall. These figures refer to different reported measures and should not be treated as interchangeable. The approach recognised that children’s safety depends on more than what happens in classrooms. Access to trusted adults, community services and safe places to spend time can also matter, particularly in areas affected by violence and social disadvantage. However, the number of people trained or children using these spaces should be understood as programme reach, rather than proof on its own that violence has fallen across the communities involved.You use AI every day. articles.title: Woman who bought a £10 ring at a London flea market and wore it for decades saw its 26.27-carat diamond sell for £656,750
articles.summary: Imagine slipping a cheap, grubby cocktail ring onto your finger, wearing it regularly for many long decades, and never suspecting that it hides a fortune.
articles.body: Imagine slipping a cheap, grubby cocktail ring onto your finger, wearing it regularly for many long decades, and never suspecting that it hides a fortune. That is precisely what happened to one woman, who paid just ten pounds for a dull-looking ring at a West London car boot sale, which Americans call a flea market. Thirty years later, a local jeweller's glance, a detailed laboratory report and a frenzied London bidding room transformed her bargain into a viral story that made international headlines. This article explains where the ring came from, what experts discovered, and why such a find is possible.How a £10 bargain at a West London car boot sale in Isleworth led to an unexpected diamond discoveryIn the late 1980s, according to Sotheby's, a woman was browsing a car boot sale in Isleworth, West London, when a box of costume jewellery caught her eye. She was drawn to some bangles, and paid little attention to a cocktail ring holding a single clear stone. Sigee writes that the ring sat in a rusty old setting and looked dull and filthy, nothing special at all. The seller wanted twelve pounds for the whole lot, and the buyer haggled the price down to ten pounds. The bangles and the ring went home with her. The Guardian, reporting through the Press Association, confirms that the ring was bought in the 1980s and that its owner believed it was a decorative costume jewel.Why the ring looked worthless for thirty years and how a local jeweller suspected a genuine diamondFor three decades the ring was simply an everyday piece of jewellery. Sotheby's reports that its owner wore it regularly, as anyone might wear a cocktail ring, convinced it could not be worth anything. Only in 2017 did she take it to a local jeweller, who immediately sensed something special. He suspected a genuine diamond but found it too large to measure accurately, so she telephoned Sotheby's. Jessica Wyndham, Sotheby's Head of High Jewelry in Europe, told Sigee that few people imagine they are carrying a stone of such size, adding that "if you've always believed something isn't valuable, there's little reason to question it." Wyndham also explained that the mount, a blend of silver and gold typical of the late nineteenth century, tarnished over time, leaving it darker and duller than modern settings.What the Gemological Institute of America report revealed about the 26.27 carat cushion cut diamondSotheby's sent the piece to the Gemological Institute of America for evaluation, and Sigee reports that the verdict was striking. The cushion-cut diamond weighs 26.27 carats, carries a colour grade of I and earns an impressive clarity grade of very, very slightly included, level two. The Guardian, in its Press Association report, adds that the stone is thought to have been cut in the nineteenth century, although its history and how it arrived at the Sotheby's sale remain unknown. The older cuts were fashioned to display fire, the splitting of light into spectral colours, whereas modern diamonds are cut to maximise brilliance. She said these proportions give a distinctive personality that collectors now find especially appealing. She added that on first seeing the diamond in person, it was clear the stone was special.How the bidding at the sale pushed the Tenner diamond to £656,750After the diamond was confirmed as genuine, the story went viral and made international headlines. The Guardian reports that the sale took place in London and that the stone was snapped up for close to twice that figure, at £656,750, a life-changing sum for its owner according to Sigee. Wyndham said, in comments carried by the Press Association, that it was a thrill to bring the hammer down on two much-discussed objects and see that attention turn into strong bidding competition. The second object was a Cartier diamond brooch worn by Margaret Thatcher, which achieved £81,250 against an estimate of £25,000 to £35,000, with proceeds going to the Endeavour Fund, a charity supporting wounded, injured and sick servicemen and women.What the Tenner diamond teaches collectors about checking old jewelleryThe story also carries practical lessons. Sotheby's has handled jewels found hidden in old curtains, tucked into chair upholstery and uncovered beneath floorboards in forgotten garages, though she stressed that the Tenner diamond is remarkable for its size, quality and extraordinary circumstances. For anyone inspired to search a relative's jewellery box, she recommended looking for signatures in the mounts or stamps on the pieces themselves, which are the clearest clues to when an item was made, who made it and its level of quality. Sigee adds that every Sotheby's jewellery specialist is a gemologist who can identify the key characteristics of gemstones. The diamond's former owner still attends car boot sales regularly, knowing treasures may hide in unlikely places.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Anti-CEC protest: Congress chief Kharge dons Batman mask during march to Supreme Court
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge was seen donning a Batman mask on Monday while marching towards the Supreme Court to file a plea against poll
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge was seen donning a Batman mask on Monday while marching towards the Supreme Court to file a plea against poll body chief Gyanesh Kumar.Kharge, who was sitting next to Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi, wore the superhero mask, which has become a trend in protests taking place around the world.However, this was not the first time the Congress had come up with the idea of using Batman for its political messaging.In August, posters portraying Rahul Gandhi as the “real-life Batman” was put up outside the Congress headquarters in Delhi.The posters feature the message, “The silent guardian, a watchful protector. LoP Rahul Gandhi, the real life batman.”Earlier this month, Rahul Gandhi launched an “Ask Me Anything” session inviting young people to question him on topics ranging from student protests and education to politics and philosophy. Announcing the initiative on X, Gandhi wrote, “Students, Gen-Z -- I'm here to listen."Ask me anything on Instagram, and I'll answer as many questions as I can.” One of the questions asked, “Are you Batman?” Gandhi appeared to play along with the long-running social media meme comparing him to the fictional superhero.“Let’s just say that no one has ever seen me and Batman in the same room together,” Rahul replied.Opposition stalwarts, along with hundreds of supporters and activists, undertook their "March for Democracy" to the Supreme Court on Monday on a heavily barricaded route and filed a joint petition against SIR and alleged poll irregularities, in another show of strength after a series of street protests over the "vote chori" charge.Rahul Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, TMC supremo Mamata Banerjee, CPI's D Raja, CPI-M leader M A Baby, RJD's Tejashwi Yadav, besides NCP-SCP leader Supriya Sule, were among those who joined the march.A day after the Chief Justice of India (CJI) declined a request for a meeting with the LoPs on the issue, saying the matter is sub judice, the opposition leaders filed the joint plea in the apex court over alleged large-scale voter deletions and irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The opposition leaders had said they wanted to hand over a memorandum to the CJI demanding an end to vote chori, Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar's resignation, halting of the SIR of electoral rolls and switching back to the paper ballot format.As police stopped the march at Bhagwan Dass Road, several leaders, including Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Tejashwi Yadav and Akhilesh Yadav, climbed atop a vehicle and the procession moved forward after crossing the barricades, as supporters cheered and waved flags.In a charged atmosphere, leaders and their supporters raised slogans against the government, CEC Kumar and asserted that "vote chori" and SIR exercise would not be allowed.A large number of supporters had already reached the Barakhamba Road junction at Connaught Place, from where they marched a few kilometres towards the Supreme Court with Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra leading the protesters along with AISA chief Neha Bora.Shiv Sena-UBT leader Sanjay Raut, CPI-ML leader Dipankar Bhattacharya and IUML leader E T Mohammed Basheer were among those present, besides Karnataka chief minister D K Shivakumar, Himachal Pradesh chief minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu and Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy (all from Congress).Get the latest India News and Live updates.
